section.title: At the Feast of Tabernacles
section.sectionRationale: At the autumn Feast of Tabernacles the tension around Jesus sharpens into open division. His own brothers do not believe; the crowds whisper; the leaders send officers to arrest Him. In the middle of it all Jesus teaches that His message is from the Father, and on the great final day, amid the feast's water ceremony, He cries out the offer of living water, the Spirit for all who believe. The crowd and the council are split, and even the arresting officers come back empty-handed and amazed.
section.thesis: At the Feast of Tabernacles Jesus teaches with an authority that is from the Father and not His own, and on the last great day He offers the living water of the Spirit to all who thirst and believe, so that the feast becomes the setting for a decisive division over whether He is the Christ.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the unbelief of Jesus' brothers and His going up in secret; His temple teaching on whose glory He seeks and why they seek to kill Him; the debate over whether He is the Christ and His words about going away; and the offer of living water, the division in the crowd, and the leaders' contempt answered by Nicodemus.

units.label: My time has not yet come
units.note: even His brothers did not believe

verses.text: After this, Jesus traveled throughout Galilee. He did not want to travel in Judea, because the Jews there were trying to kill Him.
However, the Jewish Feast of Tabernacles was near.
So Jesus’ brothers said to Him, “Leave here and go to Judea, so that Your disciples there may see the works You are doing.
For no one who wants to be known publicly acts in secret. Since You are doing these things, show Yourself to the world.”
For even His own brothers did not believe in Him.
Therefore Jesus told them, “Although your time is always at hand, My time has not yet come.
The world cannot hate you, but it hates Me, because I testify that its works are evil.
Go up to the feast on your own. I am not going up to this feast, because My time has not yet come.”
Having said this, Jesus remained in Galilee.
But after His brothers had gone up to the feast, He also went, not publicly, but in secret.

units.label: Teaching in the temple
units.note: My teaching is not My own

verses.text: So the Jews were looking for Him at the feast and asking, “Where is He?”
Many in the crowds were whispering about Him. Some said, “He is a good man.” But others replied, “No, He deceives the people.”
Yet no one would speak publicly about Him for fear of the Jews.
About halfway through the feast, Jesus went up to the temple courts and began to teach.
The Jews were amazed and asked, “How did this man attain such learning without having studied?”
“My teaching is not My own,” Jesus replied. “It comes from Him who sent Me.
If anyone desires to do His will, he will know whether My teaching is from God or whether I speak on My own.
He who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory, but He who seeks the {{doxa|glory}} of the One who sent Him is a man of truth; in Him there is no falsehood.
Has not Moses given you the law? Yet not one of you keeps it. Why are you trying to kill Me?”
“You have a demon,” the crowd replied. “Who is trying to kill You?”
Jesus answered them, “I did one miracle, and you are all amazed.
But because Moses gave you circumcision, you circumcise a boy on the Sabbath (not that it is from Moses, but from the patriarchs.)
If a boy can be circumcised on the Sabbath so that the law of Moses will not be broken, why are you angry with Me for making the whole man well on the Sabbath?
Stop judging by outward appearances, and start judging justly.”

units.label: Is Jesus the Christ?
units.note: where I am, you cannot come

verses.text: Then some of the people of Jerusalem began to say, “Isn’t this the man they are trying to kill?
Yet here He is, speaking publicly, and they are not saying anything to Him. Have the rulers truly recognized that this is the Christ?
But we know where this man is from. When the Christ comes, no one will know where He is from.”
Then Jesus, still teaching in the temple courts, cried out, “You know Me, and you know where I am from. I have not come of My own accord, but He who sent Me is true. You do not know Him,
but I know Him, because I am from Him and He sent Me.”
So they tried to seize Him, but no one laid a hand on Him, because His {{hora|hour}} had not yet come.
Many in the crowd, however, believed in Him and said, “When the Christ comes, will He perform more signs than this man?”
When the Pharisees heard the crowd whispering these things about Jesus, they and the chief priests sent officers to arrest Him.
So Jesus said, “I am with you only a little while longer, and then I am going to the One who sent Me.
You will look for Me, but you will not find Me; and where I am, you cannot come.”
At this, the Jews said to one another, “Where does He intend to go that we will not find Him? Will He go where the Jews are dispersed among the Greeks, and teach the Greeks?
What does He mean by saying, ‘You will look for Me, but you will not find Me,’ and, ‘Where I am, you cannot come’?”

units.label: Rivers of living water
units.note: the offer of the Spirit and the division it brings

verses.text: On the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood up and called out in a loud voice, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink.
Whoever believes in Me, as the Scripture has said: ‘Streams of {{hydorzon|living water}} will flow from within him.’”
He was speaking about the {{pneuma|Spirit}}, whom those who believed in Him were later to receive. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.
On hearing these words, some of the people said, “This is truly the Prophet.”
Others declared, “This is the Christ.” But still others asked, “How can the Christ come from Galilee?
Doesn’t the Scripture say that the Christ will come from the line of David and from Bethlehem, the village where David lived?”
So there was division in the crowd because of Jesus.
Some of them wanted to seize Him, but no one laid a hand on Him.
Then the officers returned to the chief priests and Pharisees, who asked them, “Why didn’t you bring Him in?”
“Never has anyone spoken like this man!” the officers answered.
“Have you also been deceived?” replied the Pharisees.
“Have any of the rulers or Pharisees believed in Him?
But this crowd that does not know the law, they are under a curse.”
Nicodemus, who had gone to Jesus earlier and who himself was one of them, asked,
“Does our law convict a man without first hearing from him to determine what he has done?”
“Aren’t you also from Galilee?” they replied. “Look into it, and you will see that no prophet comes out of Galilee.”

doxa.gloss: Glory, honor, reputation. Jesus draws a line between the false teacher who seeks his own glory and the true one who seeks the glory of the One who sent him. Because Jesus seeks the Father's glory rather than His own, His words carry the ring of truth. In John, glory finally shines at the cross, the hour when the Son is glorified.

hora.gloss: Hour, appointed time. Twice in this chapter the crowd cannot seize Jesus because His hour has not yet come. In John the hour is the fixed, Father-appointed moment of His death and glorification; until it arrives no human hand can touch Him, and when it comes He lays down His life willingly. His timing, not His enemies', governs the story.

hydorzon.gloss: Living water. At the feast's water-drawing ceremony Jesus cries that whoever believes in Him will have streams of living water flowing from within. It is the same gift He offered the Samaritan woman, now identified plainly as the Spirit. The believer not only drinks but becomes a channel of life to others.

pneuma.gloss: Spirit. John explains that the living water is the Holy Spirit, whom believers would receive once Jesus was glorified. The gift of the Spirit is tied to the completion of Jesus' work in death, resurrection, and exaltation; only then are the rivers of living water poured out on all who believe.

basic.context: The setting is the Feast of Tabernacles, an autumn pilgrim feast recalling Israel's wilderness journey and celebrated with daily ceremonies of water and light. Jesus' own brothers, not yet believing, urge Him to go public in Judea. He goes up quietly, then teaches openly in the temple, insisting His message comes from the Father, not Himself. The crowd is split, some think He is the Christ, others object that He comes from Galilee, and the leaders send guards to arrest Him. On the climactic day Jesus stands and offers living water, the Spirit, to all who thirst. The guards return unable to arrest a man who speaks like no one else.
basic.hermeneutics: Notice the theme of division: the same Jesus draws faith from some and hatred from others, and the feast becomes a courtroom where people judge Him and are judged by their response. The key questions are, is His teaching from God, and where does the Christ come from. Jesus answers that anyone willing to do God's will can recognize His teaching, and He offers Himself as the source of the Spirit. The living water is explicitly the Spirit, given after Jesus is glorified.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter turns on several terms. Jesus seeks not His own doxa, glory, but the Father's, which marks Him as true. His enemies cannot seize Him because His hora, His hour, has not yet come. On the last day He offers hydor zon, living water, which John identifies as the pneuma, the Spirit, to be given once Jesus is glorified.
basic.typology: The Feast of Tabernacles, with its water-drawing ceremony recalling water from the rock, is fulfilled as Jesus offers the living water of the Spirit. The wilderness feast that looked back to God's provision now points to the greater provision in Christ.
basic.christ: Christ is the sent one whose teaching is the Father's, who seeks the Father's glory, and who cannot be seized until His hour. He is the source of living water, the Spirit, for all who thirst and believe. The whole feast finds its meaning in Him.
basic.god: God is the Father who sends the Son and whose glory the Son seeks. He is true, and He governs the timing of events so that no one can touch the Son until the appointed hour. He is the giver of the Spirit through the glorified Christ.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 17 and Numbers 20 recall water from the rock. Zechariah 14 links Tabernacles with living waters flowing from Jerusalem. Micah 5 foretells the Christ from Bethlehem. John 4 first offered the living water.
basic.oneStory: At the feast that remembered God's provision in the wilderness, Jesus reveals Himself as the true rock from which living water flows, the Spirit for all who believe. The division He provokes runs through the whole story, as some receive the sent Son and others reject Him, unable even to see where the Christ truly comes from.

context.literary:
John 7 is a chapter of three movements, each set at a different point in the feast. Before it begins, in verses 1 to 13, Jesus is in Galilee, arguing with his brothers and then going up in secret. Midway through, in verses 14 to 36, he teaches in the temple courts and the debate takes place in the open. On the last day, in verses 37 to 52, he cries out his invitation and the chapter ends in division and a stalled council. The movement is from concealment to proclamation, and from rumour to confrontation.

The chapter is written as a series of overheard conversations. Nobody speaks to Jesus without also speaking about him. The brothers talk to him in verse 3, the crowds whisper in verse 12, the Jerusalemites reason aloud in verses 25 to 27, the people ask one another in verses 35 and 36, and the council questions its own officers in verses 45 to 52. The reader is placed in the crowd, as one of those who must decide.

Notice the pattern of failed arrests. In verse 30 'no one laid a hand on Him,' in verse 32 officers are sent, and in verse 44 the phrase returns almost word for word. The charge hangs over the whole chapter and is never allowed to land, which is the narrator's way of saying that Jesus controls his own timing. The failed arrest also forms the frame for the central claim, the offer of verses 37 and 38. It is made in the full knowledge that the powers want him silenced.

Irony drives the debate about origins. The crowd says 'we know where this man is from,' verse 27, the council says 'no prophet comes out of Galilee,' verse 52, and both are wrong in ways that the reader can see. Verse 39 gives the narrator's own commentary, so that the offer of water is explained inside the story, and the chapter ends where Nicodemus, who had come by night in 3:2, speaks up in daylight for the first time.
context.historical:
Tabernacles, called Sukkot, fell on the fifteenth day of the seventh month and ran for seven days, with a solemn assembly on the eighth, Leviticus 23:34 to 36. The Israelites were to live in booths made of branches 'so that your descendants may know that I made the Israelites dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt,' Leviticus 23:43. It was also a harvest festival, a time of great rejoicing, Deuteronomy 16:13 to 15, and the three pilgrim feasts drew crowds from all over the land. Jerusalem would have been full of people, which is why the Jerusalem crowd and the pilgrims are mixed together in the chapter.

The feast also carried prophetic expectations. Zechariah 14 looked ahead to a day when 'living water will flow out from Jerusalem,' Zechariah 14:8, and when the nations would 'go up year after year ... to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles,' Zechariah 14:16. Ezekiel saw a river flowing from beneath the temple threshold toward the east, Ezekiel 47:1, and Joel spoke of a spring flowing from the house of the LORD, Joel 3:18. Prayers for rain at this season gave the feast an agricultural edge, since the autumn rains were about to begin and Zechariah 14:17 ties rain to worship at the feast.

Later rabbinic writings, the Mishnah among them, describe a daily ceremony in which a priest drew water from the pool of Siloam in a golden flask and poured it at the altar to the sound of singing, and they speak of the joy of the water drawing, with Isaiah 12:3 as its text: 'With joy you will draw water from the springs of salvation.' These descriptions were written down after the temple fell, so they must be used with care, but the connection explains why the cry of verse 37 would have been heard. Which day is meant by 'the last and greatest day' is debated, since it could be the seventh day or the eighth, Leviticus 23:36.

The setting in the narrative is hostile. Since 5:18 the authorities in Jerusalem had sought to kill Jesus, which is why in 7:1 he stays in Galilee. His brothers, who did not believe, urge him to go up, verses 3 to 5, although one of them, James, would later be a leader of the church, Acts 1:14 and 1 Corinthians 15:7. Galilee, in the north, was despised by the Judean establishment, which colours the debate in verses 41 and 52.
context.canonical:
The chapter draws on three streams of Old Testament water. The first is the rock in the wilderness. When Israel was thirsty, God said to Moses, 'when you strike the rock, water will come out of it for the people to drink,' Exodus 17:6, and Numbers 20:11 tells how the water gushed out. Psalm 78:15 and 16 recalls how he 'brought streams from the stone and made water flow down like rivers.' Paul says that Israel 'drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:4.

The second is the prophetic picture of water flowing from God's house, in Ezekiel 47:1 and 9, Joel 3:18 and Zechariah 14:8, in which the stream brings life wherever it goes. The third is God's own title: 'the fountain of living water,' Jeremiah 2:13 and 17:13. The people who forsook him dug cisterns that held nothing. When Jesus says 'let him come to Me and drink,' verse 37, he steps into the place that Jeremiah gave to the LORD.

The gift of the Spirit, which John explains in verse 39, is the promise of Isaiah 44:3, 'I will pour water on the thirsty land ... I will pour out My Spirit on your descendants,' of Ezekiel 36:26 and 27, 'I will put My Spirit within you,' and of Joel 2:28. It comes true when, exalted to the right hand of God, Jesus 'has received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and has poured out what you now see and hear,' Acts 2:33. The first sip of this water was offered in John 4:10 and 14, to the woman at the well, and the last invitation stands in Revelation 22:17: 'let the one who is thirsty come.'

The question of where the Christ comes from is answered in Micah 5:2, which names Bethlehem Ephrathah, quoted in Matthew 2:5 and 6. John does not tell the nativity, and lets his readers recognise the irony. Even the dwelling in booths finds its fulfilment, since the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and in the end 'the dwelling place of God is with man,' Revelation 21:3.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wants his readers to hold two things together: the hostility Jesus faced, and the invitation he gave in the middle of it. The chapter shows Jesus declining to be managed, by his brothers, by the crowds or by the authorities, and it makes plain that his timing, his teaching and his offer all come from the Father. His claim in verse 16 that his teaching is not his own is not modesty. It is the credential on which everything depends, and verse 17 invites his hearers to test it by willing to do God's will.

John also writes to show what the division means. By setting the debate on the last day and in the mouths of ordinary people, he makes it clear that the issue is not a matter of information. Both sides of the argument had the Scriptures and the same facts about Galilee and Bethlehem, and they reached opposite conclusions. The difference lay in whether a person was willing to come and drink. Readers who stand outside the story are meant to ask where they stand.

The explanation of verse 39 is the narrator's gift to the reader. John wants us to know that the living water is not a metaphor for good teaching but a person, the Spirit, who would come after Jesus was glorified, so that those who read the Gospel after the resurrection can know that the offer is still open, and that they live in the age when the promise has been kept.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes how one feast went, with its rumours, its arrests that failed and its argument over a man's origins. It does not tell believers to avoid public gatherings, to travel in secret or to expect a particular day for revelation. Jesus' choice to go up quietly, verse 10, is a decision about his own hour and not a rule about how to attend worship.

Several things are prescriptive. 'If anyone desires to do His will, he will know whether My teaching is from God,' verse 17, is a principle for every seeker: obedience of heart opens the door to understanding, and a heart that wants to keep its own way will always find reasons for doubt. 'Stop judging by outward appearances, and start judging justly,' verse 24, is a command to all who judge, and it echoes Leviticus 19:15 and Deuteronomy 1:16 and 17. The invitation of verses 37 and 38 is for all who thirst, and it has never been withdrawn.

It is also worth noticing what the chapter does not command. The Pharisees' contempt for 'this crowd that does not know the law,' verse 49, is described to be exposed, not copied. Nicodemus' cautious defence, verse 51, is held up as a small, honest step and not as the finished article.

debates.question: Why did Jesus say He was not going up to the feast and then go?

views.label: He refused to go up in the manner and on the timetable they demanded
views.case: His brothers wanted him to 'show Yourself to the world,' verse 4, and he would not follow their plan. He goes later, 'not publicly, but in secret,' verse 10, so he did not act on their terms. The BSB footnote notes that some early manuscripts read 'I am not yet going up' in verse 8, which removes the difficulty.

views.label: A matter of the appointed time
views.case: The word for time in verses 6 and 8, kairos, speaks of the right moment. His refrain 'My time has not yet come' governs the scene, and he acts only when the Father directs, so that the going is hidden and the hour is the Father's, not the world's.

views.label: A genuine change of plan
views.case: A few readers think Jesus really did change course after the brothers left, as a man might. John does not say so, and since 'I am not going up to this feast' in verse 8 is plainly about their kind of going up, the text itself does not require this.

debates.bearing: None of the readings makes Jesus deceive his brothers. He refused to go up in the manner they wanted, and went when the Father's time came, which is the whole point of the hour in John.

debates.question: From whom do the streams of living water flow, the believer or Christ?

views.label: From within the believer
views.case: The BSB reads 'Whoever believes in Me ... streams of living water will flow from within him,' verse 38. On this reading the believer, having drunk, becomes a channel of life to others, which fits 4:14, where the water 'will become in him a fount of water springing up.'

views.label: From Christ himself
views.case: Some read verses 37 and 38 so that the one who drinks is the believer and the stream flows from Christ's own body, and so the true rock and temple. The Greek says 'out of his belly,' and the antecedent could be either. The picture of water from the temple in Ezekiel 47:1 and the later pierced side in John 19:34 support it.

debates.bearing: Both agree that the Spirit comes from Jesus, and that the water is a gift to be received before it is passed on. The believer is a recipient first and a channel only because of what has been received.

debates.question: Which Scripture does verse 38 quote?

views.label: A stream from the temple or Jerusalem
views.case: Ezekiel 47:1 to 9 and Zechariah 14:8 describe water flowing from the temple and Jerusalem, and the Tabernacles setting makes these likely texts. This fits the reading in which the stream flows from Christ as the new temple.

views.label: The rock in the wilderness
views.case: Psalm 78:15 and 16 and Exodus 17:6 describe water from the rock, which the water drawing ceremony recalled, and 1 Corinthians 10:4 identifies the rock with Christ.

views.label: A blend of several texts
views.case: No single verse says what verse 38 says. Many hold that John summarises the sense of several passages, among them Isaiah 44:3, Isaiah 58:11 and Isaiah 55:1, as 'the Scripture has said.'

debates.bearing: The passages agree in meaning: God promised to pour out life like water on a thirsty people, and Jesus says the promise is now being kept in him.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter has two words for time. In verses 6 and 8 Jesus says his kairos has not come, and in verse 30 his hora has not come. Kairos means the right or appointed moment, an opportunity. The hora, the hour, is John's special word for the time of the cross and glory, as in 12:23. Jesus' brothers have a kairos that is 'always at hand,' for any day suits them. His is tied to the Father's calendar. The BSB footnote at verse 8 records the textual variant 'I am not yet going up,' where the earlier reading has 'not,' ouk, and the later has 'not yet,' oupo, a small change that removes the apparent contradiction with verse 10.

Verse 15 asks 'How did this man attain such learning without having studied?' The word is grammata, 'letters,' and the sense is that he had not been trained in the schools of the teachers. Jesus answers in verse 16 with didache, 'teaching,' saying it is not his own. In verse 17 he adds that 'if anyone desires to do His will,' using the verb thelo, which means to will or wish, that person will know. The condition is a matter of will before it is a matter of intellect.

In verse 24 Jesus commands, 'Stop judging by outward appearances,' with a present imperative and a negative, which means to break off a habit already in place. The Greek for 'outward appearances' is opsis, what meets the eye. He then urges a just judgment in its place. The Messiah of Isaiah 11:3 and 4 'will not judge by what His eyes see,' and so those who would judge him must learn the same discipline.

The people twice say Jesus 'deceives' the crowd, verse 12 and verse 47, from planao, to lead astray. It is the verb Jesus himself uses of false messiahs in Matthew 24:5, and the charge is the most dangerous one that could be laid against a teacher. In verse 49 the Pharisees call the crowd 'under a curse,' epikataratoi, a strong word. Their contempt for the ordinary people makes the offer of verse 37 to 'anyone' more telling.

In verse 38 the phrase 'from within him' is literally 'out of his belly,' koilia, the inner life, the seat of feeling and the source. The same word is used in other places for the womb, and the sense is deep within. The officers in verses 32, 45 and 46 are hyperetai, temple servants, men whose job was to take orders. They come back without an arrest and say 'Never has anyone spoken like this man.' Finally, in verse 35 the Jews ask whether he will go to 'the Diaspora among the Greeks,' as the BSB footnote has it. The remark is unintended irony: after his glorification the message will indeed reach the Greeks, through the Spirit he promises in verse 39.

typology.type: Water from the rock, Exodus 17:6 and Numbers 20:11
typology.fulfillment: Israel was thirsty in the wilderness, and when Moses struck the rock at God's word, water came out for the people to drink, Exodus 17:6. Psalm 78:16 says God 'brought streams from the stone.' The water drawing ceremony of the feast kept the memory alive, and on the last day Jesus offers a better drink, 'let him come to Me and drink,' verse 37. Paul says the rock 'was Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:4, and that the drink was spiritual. The type falls short because the rock gave water to the body for a day, while Christ gives the Spirit, the water that becomes life within the person, and the rock that was struck once is the Christ who was struck once for all, in his death.

typology.type: The living water flowing from the temple, Ezekiel 47 and Zechariah 14:8
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel saw water flowing from the threshold of the temple toward the east, deepening as it went, and bringing life 'wherever the river flows,' Ezekiel 47:1 and 9. Zechariah 14:8 says on that day 'living water will flow out from Jerusalem.' In John the temple is Jesus himself, John 2:21, and the water is the Spirit that comes from the glorified Christ. The escalation is that what the prophets placed in a building in a city becomes a gift reaching everyone who comes to him. The type falls short because the river in Ezekiel is the sign of a temple that was to be rebuilt in a land, while the stream of the Spirit now flows from Christ to all nations, and one day the temple will be unnecessary, Revelation 21:22.

typology.type: The booths of the wilderness, Leviticus 23:42 and 43
typology.fulfillment: Israel lived in booths for a week each year to recall God's care in the wilderness, and the feast pointed toward his dwelling with his people. John 1:14 says the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' and the verb behind it is the one that means to pitch a tent. In the feast the people are reminded of a God who stays close, and in Jesus God is present in a body for the first time. Revelation 21:3 says 'the dwelling place of God is with man.' The type falls short because the booths were temporary and had to be rebuilt each year, while the presence of God in Christ is permanent, and it is in this, not in a seasonal structure, that his people finally dwell.

typology.type: The outpouring of the Spirit, Isaiah 44:3 and Joel 2:28
typology.fulfillment: God promised, 'I will pour water on the thirsty land ... I will pour out My Spirit on your descendants,' Isaiah 44:3, and 'I will pour out My Spirit on all people,' Joel 2:28. The pairing of water and Spirit in Isaiah is nearly the pairing in verses 37 to 39. Peter says at Pentecost that Jesus 'has received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and has poured out what you now see and hear,' Acts 2:33. The type falls short because in the Old Testament the Spirit came on particular people for particular tasks, while in Christ he is given to every believer, verse 39, and dwells within.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ through his claim about his own origin and mission. 'My teaching is not My own. It comes from Him who sent Me,' verse 16, and 'I know Him, because I am from Him and He sent Me,' verse 29. These are the words of a man whose whole life is one of sentness, and they set him apart from every teacher who comes in his own name. He does not seek his own glory, which is why verse 18 can call him 'a man of truth; in Him there is no falsehood.' It is a claim about integrity, but it is also a claim about identity: only someone who has come from the Father can speak with the Father's voice.

The chapter also leads to Christ by what he does at the feast. The water drawing ceremony prayed for water and rejoiced in God's provision, and at its height Jesus stands and calls anyone who thirsts to come to him. Isaiah 55:1 had said 'Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters,' and Jeremiah had called God 'the fountain of living water,' Jeremiah 2:13. For Jesus to say 'come to Me and drink' is for him to take the place the Old Testament gives to the LORD. The same offer sounded in 4:10 and 14, and it ends the Bible in Revelation 22:17.

The gift is the Spirit, and verse 39 ties it to Christ's glorification: 'the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.' In John, glory means the cross, resurrection and ascension. The living water flows because of what he will do. Acts 2:33 reports the promise kept. This is the point at which the feast and the cross belong together. The one who is not yet seized will be seized, lifted up and glorified, and from his death the stream will come.

Be careful with the irony of the origins debate. The crowd says the Christ must come from Bethlehem and the line of David, verses 41 and 42, and Matthew 2:5 and 6 shows that Jesus did. To the reader who knows, the crowd's objection becomes a confirmation. But John does not argue the point. He lets the irony stand and moves on, because the question that matters is not where Jesus was born but whom the Father has sent. The text does not need allegory here; it needs the simple recognition that every objection raised against him in this chapter turns out to be a witness for him.
study.god:
The chapter first shows God as the one who sends. The Father is behind everything Jesus says and does, and the phrase 'Him who sent Me' appears in verses 16, 18, 28, 29 and 33. The Father is true, verse 28, though the crowd does not know him, and the Son knows him 'because I am from Him.' Any picture of God in this chapter has to be read through the Son. To know the Father is to know the one who has been sent from him, and to refuse the Son is to remain a stranger to the one the crowd thinks it serves.

The chapter shows God as the one who rules time. Verse 30 says no one laid a hand on Jesus 'because His hour had not yet come,' and verse 44 shows the same restraint. The leaders, the officers and the crowds all act against him and still cannot touch him. There is a deep comfort in this for readers who face hostility: the ending of a life is not decided by the strength of the opposition but by the plan of the Father. This is not fatalism, since the same Father who holds the hour is the one who gives his Son for the world.

God is also the one who gives the Spirit. The living water is the Spirit, verse 39, and the promise comes from the God who said 'I will pour water on the thirsty land,' Isaiah 44:3. The Spirit is given by the Father through the glorified Son, Acts 2:33, so that the work of the three persons is held together in a single act. This is how worship has been shaped: we come to the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit.

The chapter holds two things in tension. God is sovereign, directing the hour and sending the Son, and yet people are responsible for how they respond. Verse 17 says that the one who wills to do God's will will know. Verse 37 says that anyone may come. There is no hint that someone who wants to drink is turned away. Worship in light of this is thirsty and grateful at once: thirsty because we have nothing to bring, grateful because the fountain is open and the Lord himself is its source. The officers' reply, 'Never has anyone spoken like this man,' verse 46, is the beginning of such worship, even if it is as yet no more than wonder.

crossReferences.note: The law of the feast: seven days in booths, branches and rejoicing, and an eighth day of solemn assembly. It sets out why the people were gathered at Jerusalem in John 7 and why a cry on 'the last and greatest day' was heard by a crowd in festival mood, Leviticus 23:36 and 40.

'With joy you will draw water from the springs of salvation.' The words belong to the rejoicing of the feast and give the water drawing its text. The cry of verse 37 meets that joy with an offer: the salvation the people sing about is available in Jesus.

God told Moses he would stand at the rock, and water would come out of it for the people. This is the root story behind the water ceremony, and Paul identifies the rock as Christ in 1 Corinthians 10:4, so that the thirst of the wilderness finds its answer in the one who now calls the thirsty.

God is 'the fountain of living water,' and his people dug broken cisterns. When Jesus calls the thirsty to himself, verse 37, he stands where the LORD stood in this verse, and his offer is the answer to the people's long folly of trusting empty cisterns.

Water flows from beneath the threshold of the temple, deepening as it goes. It supplies the picture of a source of life in God's house, which Jesus applies to himself as the true temple, John 2:21, and to the Spirit who flows from him.

On that day living water will flow out from Jerusalem in summer and winter alike, and the chapter goes on to name the Feast of Tabernacles in verse 16. The link to the feast could not be closer, and the water of verse 38 is the fulfilment of this promise.

God promises to pour water on the thirsty land and his Spirit on the descendants. The pairing explains the narrator's note in verse 39, that the living water is the Spirit, and shows that the idea is rooted in the prophets before it ever reaches Jesus.

A ruler will come from Bethlehem Ephrathah, one whose origins are of old. The crowd's objection in verses 41 and 42 quotes this expectation, and the BSB footnote at verse 42 points to it. Matthew 2:5 and 6 shows that Jesus fulfilled it.

Jonah son of Amittai is called 'the prophet from Gath-hepher,' a town in the north. The council's claim in verse 52 that no prophet comes out of Galilee is therefore contradicted by their own Scriptures, which shows that their certainty rested on prejudice and not on the text.

Jesus says to the Samaritan woman, 'If you knew the gift of God ... He would have given you living water.' The same offer is made here to a festival crowd, and the two scenes show that it is made to the outsider and the insider alike.

Exalted to the right hand of God, Jesus received the promised Holy Spirit from the Father and poured it out. This is the fulfilment of the promise John records in verse 39, which is why the Spirit could not be given until Jesus was glorified.

The Spirit and the bride say 'Come,' and the one who is thirsty may come and drink the water of life freely. The offer of verse 37 is repeated at the very end of the Bible, which shows that the invitation made in the temple has not lapsed.

study.oneStory:
From Genesis onwards water is a sign of life that God gives, and a river flows out of Eden to water the garden, Genesis 2:10. When people turned from God they lost the garden and were set to wander, and the long thirst of the Old Testament begins. Israel was brought through the wilderness, and a rock gave water when God commanded it, Exodus 17:6. The people were told to live in booths each year so that they would remember how they had depended on God, Leviticus 23:43. Each autumn they gathered at Jerusalem and prayed for rain, and the prophets promised a day when living water would flow out from the city and the nations would come to keep the feast, Zechariah 14:8 and 16.

John 7 is where the promise is answered by a person. On the day when the feast looked toward the water, Jesus stands and offers it. He is the rock, the temple and the fountain in one, and the water he gives is the Spirit, so that those who believe become people in whom the promise lives. The wilderness feast that looked back to God's provision now points forward to a greater one, and the thirst of the whole story finds its end in him.

The chapter sets up what follows with care. The hour that cannot yet come will come at the cross, and the Spirit will be given after the glorification, John 20:22 and Acts 2:33. The next scene in the Gospel, with its lamps and its question of the light, belongs to the same feast. And the division that runs through the chapter, some believing and some seeking to seize him, runs through the rest of the Gospel and through history.

The story ends where the thirst is finally met. The throne speaks, 'To the thirsty I will give freely from the spring of the water of life,' Revelation 21:6. The river flows through the new city, Revelation 22:1, and the dwelling place of God is with man, Revelation 21:3. The booths that were set up and taken down each year are replaced by a presence that does not leave. The reader of John 7 stands in the middle of that story and is asked the same question that the officers faced: will you come and drink?

quiz.q: How does Jesus answer the question of whether His teaching is His own?

options.text: His teaching comes from the Father who sent Him, and those willing to do God's will can recognize it.
options.note: Verses 16 and 17 ground His teaching in the Father and tie recognition to a willing heart.

options.text: He admits it is His own clever invention.
options.note: The opposite; He insists the teaching is not His own but the Father's.

options.text: He says only trained scholars can judge His teaching.
options.note: He says the opposite: anyone willing to do God's will can recognize it, learned or not.

options.text: He says it comes from God and He seeks the Father's glory, not His own.
options.note: True, but it omits the key test, that those willing to do God's will will know whether it is from God.

quiz.q: Why could no one arrest Jesus at the feast, despite the attempts?

options.text: Because His hour had not yet come.
options.note: Verse 30 gives this reason; the Father's appointed time governs events.

options.text: Because the crowd protected Him.
options.note: The crowd was divided; the stated reason is that His hour had not come.

options.text: Because the officers were afraid of the people.
options.note: The officers were amazed by His words, but the text grounds it in His hour, not fear of the crowd.

options.text: Because the appointed time of His death had not arrived.
options.note: True, this is the meaning of His hour, but the answer restates it without naming the hour the text emphasizes.

quiz.q: What is the living water Jesus offers on the last day of the feast?

options.text: The Holy Spirit, given to believers after Jesus is glorified.
options.note: Verse 39 explicitly identifies the living water as the Spirit.

options.text: Literal water for the thirsty pilgrims.
options.note: The offer is spiritual; John names it as the Spirit, not literal water.

options.text: The refreshment of His teaching and truth.
options.note: His words give life, but the passage specifically names the gift as the Spirit.

options.text: A river of blessing that flows from those who believe.
options.note: True to the image of streams flowing from within, but it does not name the gift as the Spirit, which is the point.

quiz.q: What was the response to Jesus among the crowd and leaders?

options.text: There was division, some believing He was the Christ or the Prophet, others rejecting Him.
options.note: Verses 40 to 43 describe the division Jesus provoked.

options.text: Everyone united in believing He was the Messiah.
options.note: The crowd was split, not united in belief.

options.text: The leaders believed but the crowd rejected Him.
options.note: It was largely the reverse; many in the crowd believed while the rulers scorned Him.

options.text: The crowd was split while the officers marveled that no one ever spoke like Him.
options.note: True and vivid, but it narrows the picture; the division ran through the whole crowd over whether He was the Christ.

quiz.q: How did Nicodemus respond to the leaders' contempt for the crowd?

options.text: He asked whether their law condemns a man without first hearing him.
options.note: Verse 51 records his cautious appeal to fair legal process.

options.text: He openly declared Jesus to be the Christ.
options.note: He did not go that far here; he appealed for a fair hearing rather than confessing Jesus openly.

options.text: He agreed that the crowd was under a curse.
options.note: The opposite; he challenged the leaders rather than joining their contempt.

options.text: He defended Jesus by calling for due process under the law.
options.note: True, but it restates the point without the specific question he raised about hearing a man first.

questions: Even Jesus' own brothers did not believe in Him at first. If you have loved ones who do not yet believe, how does it encourage you that some of them later did?
Jesus said anyone willing to do God's will would recognize His teaching as true. How might your willingness, or unwillingness, to obey be shaping what you are able to believe?
Jesus offered living water to anyone who is thirsty. What thirst in you is He inviting you to bring to Him rather than to lesser wells?
The Spirit makes believers into channels of living water to others. Who around you is thirsty, and how might God want His life to flow through you to them?
The feast forced a division: some came to Jesus, others turned away. What is keeping you from coming to Him fully, and what would it take to come and drink?

translationNotes.note: The Feast of Tabernacles; the BSB footnote explains this is Sukkot, the autumn pilgrim feast recalling the wilderness booths, also called the Feast of Booths or Shelters. Its water and light ceremonies form the backdrop to Jesus' words.
I am not going up to this feast; the BSB footnote notes some manuscripts read I am not yet going up. Jesus declines to go up publicly on His brothers' terms, then goes quietly at the Father's time.
The Spirit had not yet been given; the BSB footnote notes the Greek is literally the Spirit was not yet, meaning the Spirit was not yet poured out, since Jesus had not yet been glorified.
The expectation that the Christ comes from Bethlehem and David's line reflects Micah 5:2, cited in the BSB footnote; the crowd did not know Jesus was in fact born there.
